utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Thursday, the 23rd of October. Good afternoon to the accused, the Defence counsel, and the OTP representatives, together with all the people assisting us. Witness, yesterday you told me that you had a problem about today. When is your flight scheduled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have been informed by the appropriate unit that the plane will leave at a quarter to 5:00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's make sure you can take that flight. Mr. Prosecutor, you have 42 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you very much. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Yesterday, we were referring to Exhibit 1D 02651, and I don't think that the witness don't have any binders, any exhibits with him. If the usher can please assist on that. The small binder is the one with the -- the small has the Defence exhibits, and the exhibit I'm referring to is 1D 06251. I will ask to you, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 2651 as opposed to 6251.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: 2651, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And I will ask everyone in the courtroom -- I will ask you, Witness, if you can please pull out that exhibit from the binder, because we're going to talk about it. If you can -- or keep it there with you. And the other exhibit that we referred yesterday was -- which is --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And in the Prosecution exhibit, maybe the usher can assist, is P7319, 7319.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, just to recover from yesterday, you have told us that the documents essentially were the same, one was bearing the signature, one of the copies, the copy of the Prosecution, and the other difference was that the one bearing the signature was a document that was submitted to the competent ministry for Herceg-Bosna, and the other one was a copy that you have that you provided to the Defence about the activities of the Red Cross Mostar during 1993.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, I'm not quite done leafing through this. I want to make sure if there are any discrepancies in it. You have my reservations, but I don't know if anyone else has altered the text. Perhaps it's important for me to go through both documents again, but if you don't deem that necessary, then I can tell you that I see a discrepancy right on page 1, and I explained what the discrepancy was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: You already mentioned that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: All right. So we are going to -- for the purpose of the cross-examination, we are going to follow the document of the Defence, 1D 02651, and we don't have any discrepancy there. And, sir, you have told us that you were familiar with the Red Cross mandate through brochures, leaflets and documents that were forwarded to you or to the Red Cross in Mostar by the International Committee. This is what you have said on the 20th of October here in the courtroom at page 33429, line 10 to line 13. And you also have mentioned that regarding the contacts that you had with the ICRC, that you had contacts with the ICRC and with the delegates of the ICRC who were in charge of cooperation in your area either through meetings and conversations on your premises, on the premises of the Red Cross, or through meetings in their offices that were in various locations, both in Mostar and outside Mostar. And that's at page 33433, line 1 until line 13. Going through this exhibit, sir, we can see that in the summary, in the brief summary in the report of the activities carried out by the Red Cross in Mostar during 1993, in page 3 of the English version, bottom of the page, and page 1 and 2 of the B/C/S version, page 1D 51-0744 and 0745, starting with: "Radilo ...," it says: "We had to work without the support of others, and instead of them, we were the caretakers." And then it goes on saying that: "Many embarrassing things happened in relation to humanitarian aid." And there is a reference in page 4, second para of the English version, and page 2, third para of the B/C/S version, starting with: "Krveni ...," saying that: "There was assistance to the Red Cross and its activities. And the distribution of messages," it also said, "the tracing service was blocked by the ICRC because of inapplicable reasons as of the day of the outbreak of the war between the Muslim-Croat conflict on the 9th May 1993." If we continue with that preface on page 5 of the English version, sir, and the last para of page 3 of the B/C/S one, the page is 1D 510746, at the end of the introduction report, sir, you hoped -- on that report was called and you signed the report, that the municipal and higher Republic authorities would give you more space and participation in the joint effort to bring the conflict to an end, and that would be no hungry, neglected, or forgotten population. Otherwise, it would be a joint mistake and no one, no one, would forgive "us" for that, as it was well known -- it was well known how the international factor would react in such a case. And if we go through the report, sir, we that in attachment 1 of it, of this report, there is a report on the tracing service dating for the period January 1st, 1993 to December 31st, 1993, and they say that the work has been done according to the Geneva Convention of the Red Cross, and basically says that the activities consisted in distributing family messages to the ICRC, reunion of separated families, making records of missing and imprisoned persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Longone, could you get a bit closer to the microphone, please. You're difficult to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes, Your Honours. Shall I repeat the last part of the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: So the attachment 1 was referring to the activities of the tracing service, and then it mentioned -- listed three of those activities; distribution of family messages to the ICRC, reunion of separated families, and making records of missing and imprisoned persons. And at the end of that section, you have the activities of reunion of separated families, and after that, in page 8 of the English version, it says -- it's page 6 of the B/C/S version, and the paragraph is starting with: "Slusva vacinja [phoen]," and it says: "This service regularly kept records on cases when seriously and slighted wounded persons were exchanged, as well as in the cases of blockade and information on persons who got killed, who were murdered." It refers to exchange, you know, of civilians from Vojno that went to the Muslim side, 54, and below that it says that: "Detailed information of these events can be found in the archives of the tracing service in the book of minutes." And at the end of that same page, you have the register of missing and imprisoned persons, and the third paragraph, starting with: "Ovaj slusva [phoen]," I think, or "all the data are in the database computer as well as in the written form. In the time of the breaking out of the Muslim-Croat conflict, this service made a complete register of missing soldiers and civilians when the Office for Exchange and Missing And other Persons of Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna have not been found yet. This register is used by the committee of HVO in direct negotiations with the Muslim side." Sir, in reference to the reports that you received from the ICRC and regarding this yearly report from the whole 1993, were you aware of any report from the ICRC on the use of detainees held by the authorities of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna for work in dangerous conditions?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information of the International Committee of the Red Cross was not available to us. We were just complementing their information in relation to missing persons, missing persons identified through the messages that were exchanged, or maybe some other people reported them missing. We were putting together a list of missing persons in Mostar municipality and further afield as well, needless to say. Whoever came to Mostar could have reported someone as missing. The report would then have been recorded, and the International Committee of the Red Cross would try to trace people together with us. We'd send out messages, and then we'd normally receive confirmation to the effect that a person could be recorded as missing. So that's what all of our activity was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to address your attention, and you can keep those documents with you, to Exhibit P284, it is the first exhibit in the smaller binder -- sorry, the bigger binder from the Prosecution, 284. The bigger binder, the bigger binder, please. That one. Maybe you have to close it first, the binder. Yes, that's it, and it's in the very beginning. 284, 284. Exhibit 284. You can take the binder with you so you can look at it. All right. Sir, this is a report from the ICRC about the use of detainees held by the authorities of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna for work in dangerous conditions. It goes -- it expands throughout the whole period, or part of it because you were the president of the Red Cross for 11 years, but -- in Mostar, but from July 1992 to October 1993. And if you go through the pages of this exhibit, sir, at the introduction, page 2 of it, and it would be page 3 of the B/C/S version of it, it says that, regarding the practice in relation to detainees to warring conditions would put their physical integrity at risk, it says that the Croatian Defence Council, HVO, uses detainees, for such work has not only been noted by ICRC delegates visiting detention centres, it has also been confirmed by representatives, ICRC delegates visiting detention centres, it has also been confirmed by representatives of the HVO on various occasions. Do you recall any of your personnel, sir, confirming this practice of using -- on putting at risk the integrity of detainees?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. We're going to object to the line of this questioning, Your Honour. This report, first of all, is not addressed to this gentleman's place of work, it's not addressed to the Mostar Municipal Red Cross. It's addressed to the HVO, first of all. Second of all, there's some foundational issues that need to be addressed, because he's not working for the ICRC. He's just pointing to a section where representatives of the ICRC saw this particular practice. Now, if he wants to rephrase the question, I don't have a problem, but the way it's phrased, it's improper. It assumes facts not in evidence, and it makes attributions that are not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, my question was very clear. I didn't say that the report was addressed to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I just made an objection. I'd like a ruling. It just doesn't mean that counsel just begins to rephrase or re-asks the question. I'd like a ruling, I'd like an instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you are raising an objection on procedural grounds. You can see it's an important document. It's a Prosecution document, so your interest is that the witness should say something, rather than hinder the Prosecution. It's in your own interest, unless you don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand this practice. When I raise an objection, it has nothing to do with procedure, and if it did do something with procedure, it doesn't mean that we just simply ignore it. Whether it's procedure or substance, once an objection is raised, there is a response to the objection and then there needs to be a ruling. Otherwise, I don't have a record. It has nothing to do with whether this is their document or our document. What I'm objecting to is the form of the question. He points to a part of the document that says "ICRC," then he asks the question as if he's a member of the ICRC. That's what I object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, your objection is recorded. Prosecution, do ask a prior question. Ask whether the witness was aware of the document. If he wasn't aware, ask him whether he was made aware of the contents of the document, whether he was aware that there were detainees used as human shields, for instance, because I think that's your purpose, isn't it? So take it step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Did you hear the President? Could you please answer the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the question. I understand the reaction. We were not at all familiar with any of the activities of the International Committee of the Red Cross involving prisoners or, for that matter, anything else to do with their status, their stay there, their work in those prisons. We knew nothing about that. If we had known, we probably would have had the mandate ourselves to be there, but we didn't have that sort of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, in the same -- in the same page 2, it says that -- the last paragraph: "The following observations have been made," it says in the year in Mostar, and you see it says: "The most dangerous places being Santiceva Street, the ICRC also received several allegations about the use of detainees as human shields with HVO soldiers firing from behind them," Santiceva Street in Mostar. Sir, did you recall or any of your staff from the Red Cross in Mostar tell you about Bosnian Muslims use in Santiceva Street in Mostar as human shields or in danger of forced labour there?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. We had too many other things going on, and this kind of information did not reach us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, so did the ICRC -- didn't raise this to you in any of the meetings that you have exchanging information about people that are missing or killed or wounded for exchange purposes that you have in the report that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I'll repeat this. We kept records of missing persons based on reports from their next of kin. Their next of kin would come to us, the Red Cross. They would fill the appropriate forms. They would convey to us any information about the circumstances under which a person went missing, and this is how each and every one of those cases started. Anything that had to do with prisoners, any issues to do with what was the mandate of the Red Cross, the International Committee of the Red Cross alone now, this was not something that the ICRC ever raised with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, you're saying that you're receiving from the ICRC they will convey to you, sir, any information about the circumstances under which a person went missing. Here, there are references to people that are missing, basically, because they have been used -- or that people are being used in forced labour and that people has been used as human shields and soldiers firing from behind them. When you received that information of people that were missing, about the circumstances in which they were missing, you never received any information from them about that? You said that you didn't know anything about that. You were in Mostar from 1992 until 1998, and you don't know anything about Bosnian Muslims being used in Mostar as human shields and being killed, as president of the Red Cross of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will have to go back to our procedure, in terms of record-keeping, because it is quite apparent that this is not understood. There was the form of the International Committee, and then a person arriving to report one of their next of kin missing. They would fill out the appropriate form. The form would then be handed over to one of our officials, and there were very specific questions being asked of those persons in those forms. There were 20.000 such persons in that book alone. We categorized the missing according to the respective circumstance. That was all that we were looking into. We didn't deal with the reasons people went missing. We just wanted to convey all these messages, because we were receiving information from all over. Many of these missing persons later proved to not be missing at all. It's just that sometimes people were not aware of the fate of their next of kin, and then they would send this information to one address. The message would then travel back, and the person found would be removed from the missing persons list. There were people who were kept in these files and still recorded as missing, and there were always calls that were being sent out to track these persons down. Information would be checked by passing it on to other members of the missing persons' families to see if they were perhaps still there, were they still alive, were there anything that could still be done to trace that person, that sort of thing. What you're asking me about, we did not select information the way you suggest. We didn't select information in the way that you now want to elicit from me, and that is why I am entirely unable to reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, if you see in the same report, on page 4, under "Legal obligations of detainee authority," it clearly says that: "Whether combatants of civilians, the use of detainees for labour in dangerous places or for work of a military nature is expressly forbidden by the 3rd and 4th Geneva Convention of the 12th of August, 1949." And on page 6, sir, you have, below the title "ICRC Representations," a list of representations that the ICRC has made and the authorities there. You can see the names. I'm not going to go through all of them, but you can see there Mate Boban, Colonel Blaskic, Berislav Pusic, General Petkovic, and page 7 of the same report you have the conclusion saying that the authorities of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna are in breach of their international humanitarian obligations by using prisoners to work on the frontline. Violations of international humanitarian law have been numerous since the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and have resulted in hundreds of injuries and dead." And then there is the ICRC recommendation, which basically says to stop with that practice. Sir, would you, as president of the -- as the former president of the Red Cross Mostar from 1992 until 1998, would you agree with the report of the Red Cross Committee that those were unlawful practices?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't possibly judge this report. Firstly, I've never seen it before. Secondly, it wasn't addressed to the Red Cross. The institutions invoked in the document could perhaps give you an assessment as to whether that actually happened or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, let's move to Exhibit P02579.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can I send this one back or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: You can do that.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the number for me? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Yes. P2579. And you don't need to move them out from -- just take the binder with you, sir. Just take the binder with you. You don't need to move them out, so we can go quicker. 2579. If we can address attention to paragraph 11, that's in page R022-4797 of that report. Do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number is for the English version, and I need its translation. I'll see what I can find on the screen. Yes, I've got it, if that's what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Paragraph 11, sir, of that exhibit, and you have the page in B/C/S, it says: "On the 23rd May --" this is a report from the European Committee of Service, the European Community of Service, ECMM, from the 23rd to the 30 May, 1993, regarding humanitarian activity in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, and it reports that: "On the 23rd May, Grude reported that ICRC has reported that two Muslims were arrested by the HVO in the ICRC office in Mostar this morning while they were completing family message forms. There were no ICRC delegates present, only local staff. ICRC will protest accordingly." Sir, you were saying that the ICRC couldn't or had problems in distributing messages, family messages. Do you recall any incident of Bosnian Muslims arrested while they were trying to send messages to their families in Mostar in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told you that the ICRC was not distributing messages. Those messages could be filled out in the offices of the Red Cross or you could take them home and fill them out, and you could bring them to any of the addresses to be forwarded further afield. What context did you take this out from, I really don't know. I don't know what you're talking about. The situation was different at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, my question was -- it was very simple. Do you recall any incident where Bosnian Muslims, when they were filling up messages, family form in Mostar, were arrested by the HVO? Do you recall any incident? That was my question. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this before. I have no information about this whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit P02321, then. Sir, this is an order dated 12th May 1993 from Mostar. It was shown to you or it was referred to you before by counsel. You told us before that you had been a couple of times in -- earlier on, and here in the order, it says that: "At the intervention by Marinko Simunovic, representative of the Red Cross, and with the authorisation from Mr. Berko Pusic, Mustafa Mujezinovic shall be released immediately: "The above-mentioned was taken over by Mr. Marinko Simunovic," and there is your signature, sir, in the document, and it's signed by Stanko Bozic, the warden of the Mostar Central Military Remand Detention in Heliodrom. Was this Bosnian Muslim person taken out by you at the Heliodrom, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I took him over, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: You did succeed to release this person from the Heliodrom. You went there to Heliodrom and you release him?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a good reason for that. When I learned that this gentleman is the man who received me as a refugee, me and my wife, before my wife left to rejoin our children, I was so excited and moved and I sought ways to help this man get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Was he in a good shape, his physical condition, this person?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was just upset for being there. Otherwise, his health condition and everything else was in good order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Did you see, sir, other detainees at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This person came and met me outside and got into my car. I never entered the area where he had been before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Let's move to another exhibit, P04352.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: This document, do you got it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: 4352. This is a document dated Mostar, 20 August 1993. It's addressed to Mr. Bruno Stojic from Mr. Stanko Bozic, actually, and, sir, in your report it said that the ICRC was not distributing or block the distribution of messages from the Red Cross. That's what it says in the report from 1993. And here it says that: "I am writing you to inform you of the visit of the International Committee of the Red Cross to the Central Military Remand Prison and the objections they made to me. "On 11 August 1993, the Red Cross started work on registering all the detainees, and the following two days they took messages. When they finished their work in the prison, a representative of the delegation, Mr. Franco Faro, and I, as the prison warden, had a conversation. Mr. Franco pointed to the following wrongdoings and violations of the Geneva Conventions: Sending detainees to work; the quality and quantity of food; bad conditions in solitary cells. "And the representative of the ICRC warned that he was obliged, the warden, to make sure that these wrongdoings are not repeated in the future or he will be reported to the International Tribunal. On the contrary, the number," and then the warden says: "On the contrary, the number of wounded and killed at the workplace is increasing by day. Although I, as a warden, do not decide on taking detainees to work, the authorities were handed over to Mr. Vladimir Primorac, I will be held responsible before the International Tribunal. Please help us to resolve this problem in this new situation so we could protect the Central Military Remand Prison, the HVO Command and the interests of our whole people." And then it's signed by Stanko Bozic. Sir, when you pick up this person that -- this Muslim person that gave refuge to you and your family, did he told you about all these wrongdoings? Did you have a discussion about that, about the conditions in the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I have to clarify one situation relative to the role of the state committee and the information in our reports. In the International Committee --

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: I understand that. My question was: You picked up a person that was arrested at the Heliodrom. I am the one putting the questions. Excuse me, sir. We don't have that much time, otherwise I would allow you, but my question was: We see all these enunciations. Did the person that you pick up told you about all the situation and wrongdoings that were going on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but I have an objection to this answer. The witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will answer. There is no problem. This person did tell me things. That person felt embarrassed because there were a lot of people in the same room. Nothing else had happened to that person while he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, let's move to Exhibit P7787, 7787.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: You have it with you, sir? So the first page of this document is a report regarding the situation at the Heliodrom. It's dated 3 February 1994, and this report relates to Bosnian Muslim detainees originally at the Heliodrom during 1993. Now, sir, the second page, this is signed by Marjan Biskic, assistant to the minister. And regarding the information, you have -- this report is written because of a letter, a representation made by the ICRC, you can see at the end of it, saying that, on page 7 of the English version, that: "The ICRC could not visit all the persons detained by the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna authorities, since a lot of them were at various locations under the compulsory work order." And then you see a reference also, copy to Marjan Biskic, Berislav Pusic, and Vladislav Pogarcic, in B/C/S 01566928 to 29. And if we move back to the document to the beginning, to the information, to the report after the first page, that's page 2 of the English version, at the end of the second paragraph, after making reference to 60 prisoners of war, it says that: "Elmir Djasvin [phoen], killed when he was performing forced labour, Elvedin Obradovic, and Osman Elezovic, who were wounded and admitted at the Mostar wartime hospital," were they still there, that's the hospital in the part of the town that your Red Cross was. And then if you go down, it says: "Through the intelligence work, in cooperation with the operative of the Mostar centre," it says that a certain person from the HVO Engineers Platoon is keeping a number of prisoners of Muslim nationality at the Centre 2 in Ricina Street location." That's in Mostar, sir. Do you have any of these incidents, Bosnian Muslims that has been wounded and taken to the Mostar hospital, because you were -- in your report, you referred to donations of blood for those that are victims and being attended at the hospital in West Mostar, and people being detained also in Mostar, Bosnian Muslims. Do you recall any of that, sir? "Yes" or "no," that's my question.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember ever having mentioned that in any of our reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Let's go to the following exhibit, 080 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Longone. Witness, the question was not whether you had put that in the report. The question was whether you had heard of this. Have you heard of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood it was that the gentleman actually said that it was contained in a report of mine, and I have no knowledge about that and I never wrote anything to that effect in any of my reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I will not check now, because maybe I am in error.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's some confusion, Your Honour, there's some confusion. The question was inartfully put. He made reference that in his report, he talked about donation of blood. That's what that issue was. And the way it was translated and when you hear it, I guess, it would appear that the gentleman thought that this -- these incidents were included in his report. So that's where the confusion lies. So it could be if we take it step by step, instead of trying to bully the witness into an answer, we might get someplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, my question: Do you recall any Bosnian Muslim that was wounded because of being used as human shield at the use at the frontlines at Mostar and been taken to the West Mostar Hospital, where the Red Cross was giving blood donations? Do you recall any of them being treated there, sir, and blood given to any of them? "Yes" or "no," that's my question.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I must say that I did not work at the hospital. There's no way for me to know who was admitted. I was involved with the work of the Red Cross, and the way you're putting things, one might assume that I could be at ten places at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Longone, you have approximately five minutes left, at best.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Let's continue with Exhibit P08078. 8078, Witness, 8078. You have the document with you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: This is a letter sent from the ICRC on the 16 March 1994 to Colonel Zeljko Siljeg, Marjan Biskic, Mr. Jadranko Prlic, prime minister from the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Mostar, General Ante Roso, commander of the HVO headquarters, Pasovina. Sir, in this letter they're referring to people detained in Vojno on the -- from 8 November 1993 until 28 January 1994. Now, these people were transferred -- 75 of them were transferred from Roloc [phoen] earlier on to Vojno, and clearly you can see there what happened to them. They were abused at the frontlines again. Prisoner had to bang his head on a stone until bleeding. He was then beaten with a metal bar. On different occasions, prisoners had to do exercises, pushups and leap-frogs. They had to bark like dogs. And there are names of people being involved in these abuses. And then the second page, referring to the ICRC at the bottom of it, mention allegations that prisoners were ill-treated in Mostar, again in Mostar, not at the Heliodrom, in Mostar, and forced to work on the frontline. And then you see what they were doing to them. One was killed by a sniper at the frontline, Jasmin Emir. Isn't it true, sir -- and then you see at the end that: "In view of the above, ICRC would like the authorities to make the necessary inquiries concerning these allegations. ICRC is willing to provide the authorities with the detailed allegations summarised above." Isn't it true, sir, that the ICRC was trying to do their best to assist in stopping all these crimes and trying to see where these people were being taken? Because in the report there are allegations that the ICRC were not doing their work. This is what you allege in your report of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to object unless a foundation is laid. How can -- this report is not addressed to the gentleman. He needs to lay a foundation. He's trying to get the gentleman to commit that the ICRC is trying to do their job. How can he possibly answer this question unless it's put to him whether he knows what the ICRC was doing or wasn't doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, did you know anything about -- anything about Vojno? Did you know anything about Vojno camp or Vojno frontline? You mentioned Vojno in your report being exchanged Bosnian Muslims at Vojno.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I repeat for the third time, anything that had to do with the detainees, those who were arrested, that was the mandate of the International Committee from my today's perspective. I would be happy to say that it would have been good had we received these reports. Maybe we could have acted differently. But they kept these reports to themselves, and I've never seen them before. What is recorded here, I cannot either confirm or deny. I am not in a position to do that because I was not informed about all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We are getting the same questions all over again, and that's why we receive the same answers. The witness has already told us his opinion about the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have answered all these questions, but you've just said something which could prove useful. You said that the ICRC did not inform you about the problems they had. Do we need to infer from this that the people working for the ICRC did not phone you up to let you know that they had problems? They didn't tell you anything whatsoever? You knew nothing about the concerns of the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not in this area, no. We could not even inquire whether there were any problems. They were very strict about their mandate, and no delegates were allowed to talk about any of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take a very simple example. Take the case of a particular family that goes to see the delegate of the ICRC and says to them, "My husband is in prison. What can I do about this?" The ICRC delegate didn't phone you up then to tell you that, "I have heard that such-and-such a person is detained"? You knew nothing about anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they did not react that way, Your Honour, not at all. We did not have any contacts with this regard. We did not discuss the subject at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is my last question. It is related to the question you put to the witness and what I said in the beginning of this cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And in the beginning of your testimony, sir, you said that you received documents that were forwarded to you by the International Committee. They are -- in the mandate of the ICRC, there are two main points. One is related to humanitarian aid, the one is the tracing of people, the missing of people, the treatment of detainees, and that's what you mention in your report of 1993. And then the second thing you said, sir, and that I read to you was that you had contact with the ICRC and with the delegates of the ICRC who were in charge of cooperation in your area either through meetings and conversations "on our premises or through meetings in their offices that were in various locations both in Mostar and outside Mostar." You were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, Mr. Longone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: You were the president of the Red Cross, Mostar, from 1992, June, until 1998. You said the ICRC was on the ground in Mostar during 1992, 1993, monitoring and assisting your work, and your answer today, sir, is that you don't remember anything, as the president of the Red Cross in Mostar in that time, 1992 to 1998, you don't remember anything about mistreatment of prisoners, the arrest of Bosnian Muslim people, the evictions, the deportations of them, any harassment to the [indiscernible], anything about the people working for the social welfare office that were arrested in the Heliodrom that were providing to you and preparing the coffee for you, as you mentioned in the beginning of this examination; you don't remember anything? That's your answer today, sir, you, as the president of the Red Cross, Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. How do you answer that question? I think his answers to all these questions have been put and have been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Could please the witness have the opportunity to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I object to the form of the question. There are numerous questions being put, there are facts that are being assumed. If that's his closing argument he can make it at the end of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: These are not closing arguments. All these are questions put to the witness and the witness answer it during the testimony here in the Tribunal, and Your Honour knows very well that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, so the question put by the Prosecutor is a very lengthy question, because he addresses a series of issues that have already been addressed. This is a question of a general nature that recaps everything, recapitulates everything. So you say you don't remember anything, and the witness will answer. What do you have to say to this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'm prepared to answer. I understood the question. Whatever was outside my mandate, and the institutions that the gentleman is asking me about, which were not within my control, and the situations that happened of which I knew nothing, I can't remember such things. I can't remember such institutions and events. There's no -- nothing to jog my memory, because I never knew anything about them. Most of the questions contained within that long question had to do with other things than my institution and my mandate. That is why the Prosecutor is putting it to me that I can't remember things. I can't remember things if I wasn't there, if none of my men were there, if I wasn't informed, if I did not receive an official report, or if I did not receive subsequent information so as to be informed. I do have an answer, and that was my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, and no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a few questions. There may be some documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me begin with, first, that you were shown an ICRC report, and that was document P00284, and of course we could see, on the very front of it, where it says that this is a confidential report that is intended only for the authorities to which it is submitted, and it goes on. I'm going to ask you one concrete question. Did the ICRC share this report with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never received this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did they invite you to any meetings where they were participating or talking with any officials or anybody concerning the issues that were shown to you in this particular report?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were then shown another report, and that's from the ECMM, and you were shown I believe it was paragraph 10. I saw a reaction from the Bench, which is why I'm going to ask you this question, because again it makes reference to the ICRC. I want to know: Did the European -- the ECMM, these monitors, did they come to you and share their report with you and the contents therein?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did the ICRC have a separate office or did they share the same office as the Mostar Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were separate, separated. The office of the ICRC was at a different address.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, there was a reaction from the Bench which seemed to me, at least, that they found your answer to be incredible, that is, that you would not have known that somebody working for the ICRC would have been harassed or picked up by the authorities, so I'm going to put it to you concrete and squarely. Did the ICRC ever complain to you about those activities that happened in their office, which was not where your offices were located?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were shown a report by this fellow Mazowiecki. I have a problem pronouncing his name, but you saw the report. Did this fellow from the UN, did he ever come around and meet with you in your office to look at your statistics or participate in any meetings at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, did he ever show up at the coordinating committee meeting to say, "Wait a minute, let's look at this data. I'm hearing thousands and thousands of people are fleeing. Let's look at your data"? Did he ever show up at any of those meetings so he could get the collective or individual views, in front of everybody, as far as the numbers of people?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you were at the meeting. As I understand it, you made notes in your notebook. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That note was shared with us, and we shared it with the Prosecution; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allowed everyone to make copies. There are no secrets in that notebook. The work of the Red Cross was no secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me look at -- let's look at 1D 02813. This is an excerpt from your notebook. This was translated last night, Your Honours, or this morning, based on the questions that were raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recognise this paper?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And whose handwriting is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I see that there's some figures there. Let's start off, first of all, do you know about when this -- these figures or this -- when you made this -- made these notes?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made these notes on the 30th of November, if I'm not mistaken. I'm not sure if this is a "2" or a "3." Perhaps we should magnify this, but I think it's a "3." However, we don't have the right sheet of paper on the screen. This is not the information, and these are not the figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... hard copy, so just work with me on the hard copy. I'm trying to get you out of here.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So let's look at these figures.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please explain these figures to us so we understand.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. At the meeting of the coordinating committee, we received word of the numbers of people in West Mostar, and this is the information, a total of 47.558 citizens, 39.614 domicile, 7.474 displaced persons, and 470 refugees. The ethnic breakdown of the total: 34.430 Croats, 9.928 Muslims, 2.460 Serbs; other, 823. If you look at this page, you have the percentages there; 72.17 Croats, 20.84 per cent Muslims, 5.16 per cent Serbs, and the rest is probably negligible, so there's just a blank square there. It also tells us that, if we look at the total number, children between the age of 0 and age 7, a total of 4.517.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Counsel is referring to an exhibit which is a diary of the witness, and it's dated 30/11/1993. The only copy in English that we have is the one of 30 April 1993, and we are opposed to this part of the testimony of the witness to be included. And if counsel wanted to discuss more items of this thicker agenda with the witness, they should have provided that to us before so we can have a look at it and be able to respond to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, it's good trial advocacy practice that when you receive notes, even when they're not in your own language, to have -- to examine them. They have B/C/S speakers. I would have at least looked at them, through a B/C/S speaker, to find out what's in the notes. Secondly, the note, this part which was translated and has been provided to everyone, it's based on his cross-examination. That's the essence, and that's the art of rebuttal or redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm receiving -- I mean, I'm being -- or the Prosecution is being accused, and there are a lot of different ways that counsel have addressed the Prosecution, and this is the B/C/S -- the original documentation that we are talking about. Do you think I'm ready to read this, that any of our B/C/S translators can help us now to do this translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Those were provided months in advance, Your Honour, months in advance, and this was based on testimony that was elicited yesterday. We discreetly went through one page, and we translated the one page based on the numbers he provided yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] let's not dwell on this issue. During cross-examination, the witness, based on the special rapporteur's report, mentioned those figures, and I myself raised the issue by asking a question, and the witness provided the figures that we have now. Based on this, Mr. Karnavas took the evidence out of his book, his notes, that he did not invent these figures because they come from the diary for the day of the 30th of November, 1993. Where do these figures come from, we don't know, but they are written in here. Please continue, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My next question: Where do these figures come from? How was it that you put them in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, given the fact there was a representative of the social welfare centre at the meeting and the centre was keeping records, this information reached us through that particular institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me go to one other document, revisit this. I brought it up. It was again brought up on cross-examination, but I want to make sure that we're clear on this point. And this is 1D 00754. If I could have the usher to assist us, I would be most grateful. This is to help the gentleman finding the document. And I just want to get back to -- I know we've looked at this document on many occasions. I'm not interested in Article 1. The Judges can read it. They can decide how to interpret it, based on the testimony. But on Article 2, I do want you to provide us some more complete testimony. It says here: "Internally-displaced persons who have moved from one local commune in Mostar municipality to another shall return to their original local commune, if it is liberated, and re-occupy their former dwellings (own houses, flats, et cetera), which are now available ..." Now, when we are talking about internally-displaced persons, yesterday you gave us a rather nice definition and explanation of what a local commune is. What are we talking about, "internally-displaced persons," in the context of Article 2 of this particular decision?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this section is concerned, it was the aspiration of the authorities for those people, who were able to return to their own liberated areas and actually had houses or flats to which they could return, to do so. It was precisely based on our records and on the records of the social welfare centre that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We understand all of that, but I want -- what do we mean by "internally displaced" versus "displaced persons"?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A person, for example, from local commune A, because of enemy activity, had to travel to local commune B. The house that this person used to own in the previous local commune had been destroyed, so this person now had nowhere to go back to. After the situation had calmed down and things were back to normal, and the house was still there, this decision ordered this person to indeed go back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So are we talking about Mostarians, basically, people from Mostar municipality? Is this what we're referring to when we say --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, from the entire Mostar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Not from other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only internally-displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand your testimony from direct, some of these individuals were double-dipping, were receiving aid twice, and that was one of the other motivating factors, based on your testimony on direct. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were cases like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were asked a series of questions today about whether you saw anybody on the frontline being used for this or that. Your work, as I understand your testimony, was primarily dealing with disbursing humanitarian aid. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to a very large extent. There were other activities; blood donations, for example, first aid, and everything else that we mentioned in our report. But for the most part, our job was about humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's talk about blood donations, because the implication is that since one of the functions was blood donations, you would have known what is going on in the hospital. Where was the blood being donated, how was it controlled, and to what extent were you aware of who was going to the hospital either to give blood or who was at the hospital receiving medical attention?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the hospital, there was a special ward or department for transfusion, and the Red Cross tried to raise the awareness of the population in terms of donating blood, in terms of becoming donors. The hospital would draw up a plan, together with us, in relation to a specific local community for all those who were prepared to go and donate blood to do so. Our objective and our mission was to raise their awareness, was to explain to them that this was a good deed and that they might save other people's lives by donating blood. We kept records of these donors. The hospital staff, the hospital, would check blood samples, check the blood type and everything else that one does when dealing with blood donations and how it is then distributed or used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. To what extent -- to what extent were you or your staff going up to the frontline, to the separation line where there was activity, to carry out your own work?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have access to the confrontation line or the frontline at all during the actual war operations. This would have been too dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I mean, the implication is that since you're the Red Cross, obviously you would have known what's happening on the frontline, if anything, and that you would be able to make these reports to the ICRC. Did you ever drive down -- up and down the boulevard that was dividing the city to figure out what's happening, who's doing what to whom and why?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I never did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, Monday it was put squarely to you that you are a member of the joint criminal enterprise, that you were deliberately trying to deny Muslims humanitarian aid. It was put to you fairly and squarely. It's there on the transcript. It was on Tuesday. Not yesterday; the day before. And I want to ask you one concrete question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you deliberately trying to deny Muslims humanitarian aid, either you individually or in your capacity as the president of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Longone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted for the record, the Office of the Prosecutor are not saying that this -- we want the transcript reference regarding where the Prosecution said that this gentleman is a member of the joint criminal enterprise. We didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He didn't have to say it. He put to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Then don't say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He put to the witness -- he put to the witness that the Mostar Municipal Red Cross was trying to deny humanitarian aid to the Muslims. It fits well within their theory, it's the overall theory, and I'm putting the question to the witness: Did he ever try to deny Muslims humanitarian aid, and if so, to describe it to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Longone, you never said that, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: I never said that this gentleman was a member of the joint criminal enterprise, and I want the reference from the record of these accusations that counsel has just made to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: By implication, Your Honour, by inference. They never -- they don't have to say that the person is a member of the joint criminal enterprise. It's by their accusations. That's why yesterday I objected to the way they're characterizing Croats. It's collective guilt that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you do a bit less shouting, Mr. Karnavas, please. It would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you or your organisation ever try to deny Muslims or anyone else humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed attorney, Your Honours, I'm free to say this loud and clear here today. The Mostar Red Cross did its job to the best of its ability. There has been a lot of evidence here that confirms that, irrespective of people's ethnic backgrounds, and without meaning to deprive anyone of aid. I will stand staunch and I will defend this truth anywhere, any time. Likewise, I would like to thank everyone, all the people who were working with us at the time, all those the whole world over who were helping us accomplish our mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One final question. When -- after the Washington Agreement, which is 1994, and after the Dayton Agreement and thereafter, all the time up until you completed your work with the Red Cross in 2003, where were you -- where were you employed, in what city?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998, I was appointed chief secretary of the Federation's Red Cross, and I remained in that position until 2003. As a representative of the Mostar Red Cross, I became a member of the working group whose mission it was to set up the federal Red Cross. On behalf of the Herceg-Bosna Red Cross, in keeping with all the agreements that were signed, I was actually involved in carrying out tasks envisaged in the agreement. As soon as the conditions were right to set up a society at the federal level, I was again a member of this inter-ethnic entity contact group with another colleague of mine from the Federation. We had a total of 33 meetings with the Serb side, the Red Cross of the Republic of Srpska, and we succeeded in preparing an Assembly of the Red Cross -- the Society of the Red Cross of Bosnia-Herzegovina, thereby making international recognition possible. From Day 1, from the day I joined the Red Cross, I was actually involved in accomplishing its mission, on the one hand. On the other, I was involved in institutionally organising the Red Cross from the municipal level all the way up to the federal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when you were trying to organise it at the federal level, was that out of Mostar, or was that out of Sarajevo, or someplace else?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was out of Mostar, until such time as the Red Cross was established, actively through these meetings, with the representatives of other municipal organisations from throughout the Federation. We reached all the elements -- or, rather, we accomplished all the elements in order to set up an assembly and set up a Red Cross for the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, thank you. Now, please get out quickly so that you can catch your plane.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you. I thank you very much for your patience. I thank all of you who have been asking me questions over the last days. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. With regard to next week's schedule, as you know, we'll start at 9.00 in the morning, and we are to have two 15-minute breaks so that we can finish at 1.00. We shall resume at 2.00 in the afternoon to finish at 4.00. And in the afternoon, we'll have 15-minute breaks as well, because there's another hearing, more or less, covered by the media scheduled to start at 4.00 in the afternoon, so we can't work after 4.00. But we'll have more than five hours and a half of hearing and then we'll have the rest of the week and the week thereafter. Is that right, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct, and I did have one bit of news for the Trial Chamber, in light of yesterday's letter that we received from the Prosecution. Actually, we had made a decision prior to receiving the letter, and I did communicate with the Prosecution our position, and I'll do so on the record and for the Trial Chamber's convenience as well. We have looked at our case, and of course we are very mindful that we need to reserve certain hours, and of course the following witness is a rather complicated witness and we may need to use an extra hour with him. We don't know. But be that as it may, we have decided, after consultations with our client as well and looking at the case map that we've been preparing ever since we began this odyssey some two years ago, that we will not be calling the four 92 bis witnesses that have testified in previous cases before the Tribunal. There are four of them. As for the remaining four, a question was raised earlier today by the Prosecutor, and I told him that our position is not to call any of them, but to merely submit their one- or two-page statement to the Trial Chamber, and I'm still waiting for the one to arrive, and when we get it we will present it to everyone. But, again, the four that have previously testified that we had on our list, we are withdrawing. So and that -- and I only mentioned it now on the record to ensure that if you are discussing scheduling matters, you can factor that into your -- into the programme. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So with the remaining schedule, there's going to be a gap in early December, since Radovanovic, this expert, is scheduled to testify in the week of the 24th to the 27th or 28th, but Mr. Stringer said that he would be in a position to cross-examine that witness. So we're going to have a gap in the beginning of December. We understand that the Stojic Defence cannot call their first witness named Davor if they haven't first heard Cvikl. We know that the report, in B/C/S, will only be translated in two months' time. It means that they won't have this report available by the 22nd of December. Davor has to be after Cvikl, I can understand that, but I'm now turning to the Stojic Defence. Don't you have other witnesses that are not so dependent on Davor, that could, for instance, be called earlier in December? Don't you have that kind of witness? Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, firstly, I'm grateful for the opportunity to address this question. It was an issue which we wanted to discuss and seek the guidance of the Trial Chamber. Of course, you are in possession of the letter, Mr. President, addressed to the Trial Chamber, dated yesterday, from Mr. Stringer. Your Honour, the first point is this: That we are looking forward, on behalf of Mr. Stojic, to starting our Defence case. He has been, of course, sitting in this dock for a long time, and he's looking forward to the opportunity to clarify some misunderstandings and some of the misconceptions of the Prosecution case in the course of the defence that he's putting on, and the sooner, in many respects, the better. Your Honour, we are -- let me make it crystal clear. We are very happy to start on the 1st of December, notwithstanding the fact that as things stood earlier this week, it was anticipated with the schedule that we then understood was in place that we'd be starting in January. However, we are adamant, in our respectful submission, that our witness, Davor, Marjan, must be our cornerstone witness, he must be the first witness that we call. Your Honour, on the 20th, Mr. President, you yourself put it very succinctly, and I quote from page 20: "Witness Davor," that is Marjan, "is in strategic terms important because he will be the cornerstone of your Defence strategy and the rest will come after that." That was put, of course, in crystal-clear terms by my learned leader in her submissions on this issue. Now, this Defence strategy hasn't been simply cobbled together in the last few months. It certainly pre-existed my joining the team at a very late stage. My learned leader has the strategy in place from the beginning of this Defence case, and in my respectful submission a very significant margin of discretion must be given to the team -- to the lead counsel of each team as to how they are putting their own case. Now, as I understand it, so important is the expert witness Marjan, it would be the most efficient use of time and the appropriate relief would be to allow us to call this witness on the 1st of December. Now, there is, after Cvikl has testified. The expert report of Cvikl was distributed to the parties, the Defence and the Prosecution, on the 10th of October. By the 1st of December, the Prosecution would have had 51 days to consider that report. It's just nine days shy of the two months that the Trial Chamber are ordering as a period of reasonable time to prepare. Now, that does not, of course, address the issue of the translation into Croatian. That, itself, was an application by the Stojic team to Mr. Karnavas, that it was required to be in Croatian. Your Honour, there are two options, in my respectful submission, that could address that particular difficulty. The first is Your Honours may collectively wish to direct the Registry to prioritise this report, because it would have ramifications to the whole scheduling of the Trial Chamber, and ask them to make this available, for example, the last week of November. They would still have three weeks plus to prepare that expert report. That's the preferred option, in my respectful submission, that the Registry be told this is a very important document, it's one that would have significant implications on the scheduling and the usage of court time, and therefore it's not beyond the wit of those in the translation services. They are very efficient and they are very capable. No doubt, they are very overworked. But if they could be directed to prioritise that document, that's my primary application and my preferred option in relation to this matter. The other option, however, is given the best use of court time, and of course we are very much alive to the efficient use of court time in the Stojic team, at least that is our hope and our endeavour, my learned leader has told -- has informed me that the other option is that we sit down with our client in the Detention Unit, with a translator, and go through that document orally with him. So that's the fall-back position. We put forward these two different options in a very sincere attempt to overcome the hurdle of the Cvikl testimony, but it's because of the extreme importance, in our submission, that we start our case with the witness of our choosing to pursue the strategy chosen by the lead counsel responsible for this case, and in our respectful submission it's a reasonable and proportionate response to overcome the difficulties that are in place. It would ensure that the court time was properly utilised. We would start on the 1st of December, Cvikl gives evidence the week before, and in our submission, all of this could work quite nicely and neatly to make sure that the time between the 1st of December and the 12th of December is not cast to the wind. Your Honours, I hope that is of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the two options suggested by the Stojic Defence are most interesting, but they do depend on the Prosecution's position regarding Cvikl, indeed. We'd like to know when you would be ready to cross-examine Cvikl. That's the problem, that's where the problem lies, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good afternoon, Your Honours. I thought it was settled, the Prosecution was going to begin its cross-examination of Mr. Cvikl on the 12th of January, and I can assure the Trial Chamber that we are not going to be in a position to address this witness any earlier. I think, actually, if the Trial Chamber's had an opportunity yet to review his report and the materials that accompany it, I think there's -- the 12th of January is a tall order, to be honest, in our view, but the 12th of January is absolutely the earliest at which time the Prosecution's ready for Mr. Cvikl. And then just continuing off of what my learned friend Mr. Khan has just been saying, if I understand correctly what's being proposed is that the Stojic -- well, I guess I understand that, in fact, the Stojic Defence still are adamant that for their strategic reasons, Mr. Davor Marjan has to testify after Mr. Cvikl. So if that is, in fact, the case, then I think there is no way that he can testify before the middle of January. That's the Prosecution position. Today is the 23rd of October. We haven't seen the expert report, it's not been filed yet, and so certainly there's no way that the Prosecution is going to be in a position to consider Mr. Davor Marjan as a witness during -- at any point during the month of December. I can assure the President of that. So as the Prosecution sees it, it has to be the witness Cvikl beginning on the 12th of January and then with the Stojic expert, Mr. Davor Marjan, the week following Cvikl, at the earliest. We still think that it's -- I guess if I could add one final point. We don't understand the link between these two expert witnesses. They're being called by different parties. One is an economist. The other one is apparently going to testify about the structure of the Department of Defence of the HVO. So it's not at all clear to us, based on what we've been told, why these two experts are linked in this way in which it's absolutely necessary to call one after the other. But, again, we haven't seen the Stojic team's report, and so we're all a little bit in the dark about what the witness is going to say. I can only assure the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution must insist on Mr. Cvikl coming the week of the 12th, which is the minimum amount of time we need. If the Stojic expert is to come, he has to come after Cvikl, and again we don't see that it can necessarily be fatal for other witnesses to be called by the Stojic team during those two weeks or so in December. And just one last point on the 92 bis witness -- witnesses that the Prlic team does intend to call, because I -- I mean, again, we haven't seen those either, we haven't seen those letters, and we understand, I believe, what the nature of those are, but we haven't seen them, and I don't want to create expectations that there will not be -- that the Prosecution will not take a position that any of those don't have to come. It's quite possible that the Prosecution may review those and take the position that one should come or more. I don't know. So that may, in fact, put us in the position of considering whether any of the remaining Prlic witnesses would need to come. So I don't want to prejudice the Prosecution position in respect of these four remaining 92 bis witnesses, because we may ask the Trial Chamber to bring one or more of those, depending on what those statements say. But in respect to the two experts, it has to be after the first of the year, as far as the Prosecution is concerned. We would ask the Trial Chamber to consider whether other witnesses from the Stojic case can nonetheless be brought to testify in December. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there's one point we can do nothing about. The Prosecutor has just said that he will not be in a position to examine Cvikl before the 12th of January. It's on the transcript. As you have just said that Davor can only come after Cvikl, we have a second date for him. Mr. Khan, we have another problem. Your expert, Davor, I haven't seen the report yet. Is it going to be filed soon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I indicated, I think, two or three days ago, I gave an undertaking on behalf of Mr. Stojic that that report would be filed by tomorrow, and in fact I sent an e-mail just a few minutes ago to the Prosecution similarly indicating that that expert report would be filed tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the second issue is concerned that was raised by Mr. Stringer, he feels that other witnesses could come and testify before Davor. You are saying that this is impossible?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, in my respectful submission, of course I'm always extremely grateful for the very experienced and very sincere advice of the Prosecution, but in this particular case, trespassing as it does to the Defence, it's perhaps better to leave it to the Defence as to how it seeks to run its case. Your Honour, the test, in my respectful submission, articulated -- the test articulated by my learned friend, that interposing other witnesses prior to our expert, Marjan, would not be fatal of course is completely erroneous. It's not a test at all. It needn't be fatal. It's of course for the Defence to decide how to call its case. And, Your Honour, it sometimes is very infantish and -- to say, well, this happened to the Prosecution and this is what happened on another case, to support a particular argument, but of course they were -- we are ready to start on the 1st of December, within the parameters that we've articulated. We do submit that they are reasonable. There were quite a few occasions, at least after I joined the Stojic case -- the Stojic team in which the Prosecution didn't have particular witnesses available of their choice, and one week was put aside or a few days were lost in the trial calender, and at least I never stood up and said, "Well, the Prosecution should bring somebody else." I left it to the Prosecution and their experience how they should put on their case to the best of their ability. And I think that same privilege, that same right, in fact, should be enjoyed by Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Mr. Prlic wanted to say something. Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a very brief intervention, Your Honour. Everyone wants to say something for the record. I would just like to state one sentence for the record. I will not go into the merit of who is right and who is wrong, procedurally, of who has sufficient time and who doesn't, does something right translating or not. But as a matter of principle, I -- all six of us are hereby condemned to another month of prison. This trial began when my child was born in 2004, in March 2004. My child is about to start going to school, and we will not have seen a judgement rendered yet. Therefore, all the time that passes for you is more or less business as usual. Sometimes business is good, sometimes not so good, but that's not my concern. But we have been spending all this time in prison, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to make an early warning, something that has already been shown to be the case in this trial. We are losing pace, to a large extent, and the trial is foreseen to be finished by the end of next year. What about us, accused number 3, accused number 4, accused number 5, accused number 6? What if we run out of time, what if we end up in dire straits and then number 5 and number 6 don't have sufficient time to do the job properly because there was someone at this point in time who required a 40-page translation and lost two months doing that? And Mr. Prlic, it's not a single month, it's two months for a mere 40 pages. My own team submitted 600 pages for translation recently. It was actually done over a 15-day period. This is just the evidence of two witnesses from this case, and that's for us who are working on it to get into this in detail. It's not just for us, it's for a more general purposes. The cost of a single page is 15 euros, just to put that on the record, and thank you for hearing me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Coric, I can reassure you, don't be concerned as far as number 5 and 6 are concerned. You have been allotted some time, and you will have some time, and you will be able to present your case. Even if the trial is not finished next year, it will be carried over into the following year. You will have enough time to call your witnesses. Of course, it is clear that things are going on for longer. This is something which we all come to realise. Personally, I would have preferred this trial to be finished already. Unfortunately, we are dependent on a series of factors, we are all dependent on a series of factors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, I must fully agree I am of the same opinion as Mr. President. We will not rush over any Defence. That is completely out of the question. The Defence of the proceedings has an absolute priority for this Chamber, and we will never sacrifice it to speediness, the more so as while, on the one hand, we understand your plight and the difficulties that you experience, and on the other hand I have also heard Defence speakers say that they wanted a fair trial even if it took a bit longer. So this is a very difficult balancing exercise. Now, as to the specific question, just not to have missed a chance, although not with great hope of a positive result, I would like to ask whether any other Defence would see the possibility of filling that gap we are facing in December. I am fully aware that it is rather unlikely, and, please, no Defence ought under any circumstances feel to be under pressure. But in case one of you ladies and gentlemen sees a possibility to bring in some evidence during these two weeks, I think it would not -- there's no absolute need that we proceed in the chronological way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak might wish to call some witnesses. Mr. Praljak, you have the floor. Seize this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They keep telling me I shouldn't. I wanted to make a proposal to take a note to appear as a witness and for everything I say to be recorded. That was the sort of agreement that we have. But, Your Honour, Presiding Judge, Judge Antonetti, with all due respect, there is no way you can guarantee that we shall actually be extending this trial. You want that, and at least speaking of myself, I told you I didn't mind the length of trial. When I said I didn't mind, well, I'd rather for the trial to go on, rather than compromising its fairness, but you have the big fish and the Security Council, the big fry, and they took a decision to shut the door on this Tribunal, and then perhaps this whole trial should start all over again in a different court of law. Despite our best efforts, for international justice to continue, this just might happen, and then they could tell you, "Listen, gents, no way you can wrap this up, shall we now all go home, please." Thank you. This is a very realistic possibility that we're looking at. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right, that would be a possibility, theoretically speaking. At any time, the Security Council may decide to stop everything, but we have no information about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to stop now, because the tapes have run out. We shall meet again, therefore, on Monday as planned. I hope that you will all strive to make things advance quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 27th day of October, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.03 p.m.,
